anti_overlap: Aviation safety inspection (covers pre-flight checklists and ASRS reporting, not rolling-window functional failure rate monitoring)
Pharmaceutical post-market surveillance (covers pharmacovigilance signal rates and NDA approval gates, not equipment reliability monitoring)
Financial audit continuous controls monitoring (covers financial-control signal rates rather than safety-critical equipment performance thresholds)
decision_lens: Prioritize findings where a gate result is used as a substitute for sustained-rate evidence. The Maintenance Rule distinguishes systems in a-category (continuous performance monitoring required because prior gate results were insufficient) from b-category (periodic inspection sufficient). If Break receipts are scored at a boundary rather than tracked as a rolling rate, the system is claiming b-category treatment for what should be a-category behavior.
distance_rationale: Nuclear maintenance rule monitoring applies the same gate-vs-continuous structural question to safety-critical equipment qualification, at regulatory scale with established jurisprudence, but for mechanical/electrical systems rather than software trust lifecycles.
expected_isomorphisms: The a-category / b-category classification maps directly to the Break-as-continuous-mode vs Break-as-gate choice: a-category requires sustained rate monitoring because a single gate is known to be insufficient evidence of ongoing health. The rolling-window functional failure rate maps to the sustained contradiction-surfacing rate proposed in option (b). The regulatory requirement to set measurable goals and monitor against them maps to the Tier-2 evidence proposal in option (b).
focus: Gate-vs-continuous health monitoring in safety-critical system qualification
name: fd-nuclear-maintenance-rule
persona: Apply the perspective of a nuclear plant maintenance engineer who implements 10 CFR 50.65 (the Maintenance Rule). They care about distinguishing a-category performance monitoring — where a system must sustain a functional failure rate below a threshold over a rolling window — from discrete inspection gates. They measure whether a system is performing its intended function reliably over time, not just whether it passed a point-in-time check. They flag any design that treats a single inspection result as a durable health certificate.
review_areas: Assess whether ≥N Break receipts at a boundary is structurally equivalent to a-category monitoring or b-category inspection — and whether the subsystem's self-observation behavior warrants which classification
Check whether the current Break spec defines a rolling observation window or only a cumulative count — Maintenance Rule monitoring is window-based, not lifetime-cumulative
Evaluate whether a subsystem that 'banks' N receipts early in Compound and then goes quiet would be detected — a-category requires sustained performance, not front-loaded compliance
Verify that the Break receipt rate, if used as Tier-2 evidence, has a defined measurement goal set before the Compound window opens — not calibrated post-hoc
Examine whether Interspect's severity scoring of Break receipts is independent enough to count as a-category monitoring or whether it is effectively self-assessment
Consider whether the ≥N gate is an appropriate simplification for M1-M2 subsystems (where b-category may be reasonable) but insufficient for M3+ (where a-category is warranted by criticality)

severity_examples.condition: When the Break spec specifies ≥N receipts in the Compound window without requiring a minimum distribution across that window
severity_examples.scenario: Break receipts are counted lifetime-cumulative with no rolling window — a subsystem banks N receipts in month 1 of Compound and is silent for the rest of the window, satisfying the gate without demonstrating sustained self-observation health

severity_examples.condition: When §7.1 does not specify that Break goals are published before the Compound window opens
severity_examples.scenario: The gate threshold N is set after Compound evidence is already collected — post-hoc calibration of the very metric used for gate passage, which invalidates the independence of the Break signal

severity_examples.condition: When the Break spec applies a uniform gate across all M-tiers and criticality levels without distinguishing which subsystems warrant continuous-mode monitoring
severity_examples.scenario: High-criticality subsystems (Governance, Routing) use the same ≥N gate as low-criticality subsystems — the Maintenance Rule would mandate a-category for critical-function equipment regardless of past inspection record

source_domain: Nuclear power plant maintenance and reliability engineering (10 CFR 50.65)
success_hints: Identifies whether the Break spec is structurally a-category (rate-monitored) or b-category (gate-only) and whether that matches the criticality of the subsystems it governs
Flags if the spec lacks a rolling-window requirement or pre-specified measurement goals, which are the two distinguishing features of a-category compliance
task_context: Reviewing §7.1 of the Sylveste vision v6 outline, which introduces a Break phase between Compound and Epoch in the subsystem trust lifecycle. The upstream judgment call is whether Break should be a discrete gate (≥N receipts before transition) or a continuous-mode requirement (sustained contradiction-surfacing rate as Tier-2 evidence about self-observation health). The reviewer brings nuclear maintenance rule monitoring practice — specifically the a-category vs b-category classification for safety-critical equipment — as a parallel professional discipline for evaluating this structural choice.
